rv.q: Archduke is a real oddity and a lingering delight.
Theatrically Joseph’s thesis graduates with high honours.
This is still an enjoyable, eccentric and immensely topical evening, delivered with enormous flair.
A delicious cackle in the dark, at a subject that’s not becoming irrelevant anytime soon.
The play seems oddly insubstantial given the subject matter, though it’s enjoyable enough in Lyndsey Turner’s production.
As the action shifts to the train to Sarajevo, the characters keep talking but the play runs out of things to say.
There was, I suppose, a play somewhere in the room but it eluded me.
Both inject their roles with unique and precise characterisation, and perfectly complement the line-up of darkly humorous characters that make this production so engaging.
Turner directs with a palpable delight in the play’s absurdism and zany sensibility.
I for one, thought it thoroughly inventive and weirdly delightful — largely due to the cast’s insistence on embodying their utterly warped and engaging characters to full effect.
A playful and passionate production.

It has its moments, but it can’t hold a candle to Turner’s previous project in terms of wit, characterisation, and thematic richness, and unfortunately ultimately registers as bit of a simplistic anticlimax.
Ultimately, Archduke succeeds most as an entertaining and inventive dark comedy that humanises the figures behind a defining historical act.
But amidst the mayhem, it’s sometimes difficult to discern what the overall point is.
Despite its unevenness, the play earns its place.
Instead, it comes across as an annoying piece of trivialisation with little new or interesting to say.
Maybe that’s the hazy message of this play, whose slight plot, superficial characters and bad comedy don’t seem to take us anywhere else.
Perhaps that's the most unsettling thing about Archduke – it reminds us how easily history can repeat itself.
Archduke is a largely breezy affair, given the subject matter, filled with physical comedy and visual gags.
However, Archduke tries to pack too much into underdeveloped characters with a lack of direction as to what the main story really wants to say.
While Archduke has the gun locked and loaded, it fails to pull the trigger, leading to a show that is on the precipice of greater success, but somehow misses, becoming more of a misfire.
Archduke is poor stuff across the board.
It’s fearless, tightly crafted theatre that sticks in the mind.

If there is a weak point here, it is American playwright Rajiv Joseph’s supposition about the ridiculous way the people behind the assassination of the heir to the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Archduke Franz Joseph, arrived at this momentous historical event.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this dark comedy about Franz Ferdinand's assassins, with many praising Es Devlin's striking set design and the contemporary resonance, but others finding the absurdist approach trivializes history with uneven execution.
